chapter: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
title: Auditioning Lu for Decca and the race-record jukebox market
summary: Mel Williams asked for something raunchier than Lu's blues, and Danny explains that Black and white jukeboxes carried different repertoires until Louis Jordan and King Cole.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So they're looking for talent. So they tell, 'Well, Decca...Mel Williams is in town, and they're looking for talent, so why don't you go down there?' So I bring Lu down there, and she's singin' the Blues. So Mel Williams says, 'Ain't you got somethin' a little raunchy?' Yeah, yeah, a little under-the-table stuff. Somethin' funky. He didn't say it like that, though. Something like...you know, like a cathouse song or something. Because in the Black market you could do that, because the records weren't played... About this race record business. They weren't played on radio, because they didn't have that many disk jockeys at the time, and they were very highly sensitive to what was put on the air. You know, you couldn't even swear. But there was a big market that the same jukeboxes... The Black jukeboxes, they would have a whole different

repertoire than White jukeboxes.
One of the first artists to play on White jukeboxes, in White joints, was Louis Jordan. After Louis Jordan, then came King Cole. When he made "Nature Boy," you found him in every hotel in the country. You would hear... He's the one that revolutionized this thing where you can hear Black artists on White... Because some jukebox owners didn't have a record... I knew some of them, because I approached them with my record. They had never had a Black record in the store. Everything was for hotels and...you know... So you had all that to go against you.
